utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit. The affirmation you made still applies. I thought you'd sat down, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I did. I'm finished. I just have an administrative issue. There was a mistake in e-court. We have notified the OTP about it. When the transcript of the witness was being uploaded, which is D011-3778, it should be D723 under seal; and D011-4037 is D724. Could we please make that correction. D723 and D724 are the new numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Paige Petersen. I'm going to be asking you some questions today.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: During 1998 and 1999 did you know the accused in this case, General Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during 1998 I saw the accused, Mr. Djordjevic, on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's break this down a little. So -- well, first let's follow that up. You saw him on one occasion in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Djordjevic in late July 1998 in the office of the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps, General Lazarevic. When I entered they were sitting down, having coffee, and engaging in an informal discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Was it a meeting, or was it just an informal talk between him and General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an informal conversation between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, did you personally know General Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know General Djordjevic personally. I did know, though, that he was chief of the public security sector of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. And did you -- so you knew who he was, although you didn't know him personally?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Was that from television or from the official capacity that you held, or how was that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about him based on the official capacity as well as through the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. And during the NATO bombing period, did you know of General Djordjevic, his official capacity at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the NATO bombing period, Mr. Djordjevic was chief of the sector of the MUP of Serbia and assistant minister to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And he had that position -- did he have that position during the NATO bombing as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he stayed in that position even after NATO bombardment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: But I just want to be clear about the period of the NATO bombardment. Is it your understanding that that was his position at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the NATO bombardment, as far as I know, he was assistant minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia in charge of public security.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And during the period of the NATO bombing, did you see General Djordjevic in Kosovo at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the bombing of the -- of the NATO Alliance, I didn't see Mr. Djordjevic in the area of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: In the capacity that General Djordjevic held, if he would have visited Kosovo, is that something that you would have known about likely?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the capacity he had at the time, I didn't need to know of his visit. However, given that he was a senior official, I believe I would have been informed of his visit to Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Were you aware of General Djordjevic visiting Kosovo on the 16th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Were you aware of General Djordjevic being in Kosovo on the 18th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is possible that Mr. Djordjevic did visit Kosovo briefly in the company of the minister of the interior, but I had no information to that extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. So I would just submit to you at this point General Djordjevic testified in his own Defence in this case and he told us that he was, in fact, in Kosovo on these two dates, the 16th and the 18th of April. So can we agree, in fact, sir, that you would not necessarily know if General Djordjevic was in Kosovo? You would not necessarily have been informed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, at this point in time as you sit here today what's your relationship with General Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no relationship. I'm merely appearing as a witness in his Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, so he's not someone who you know very well or at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't quite agree with you. He's not someone I know well, but he's not someone I don't know at all either. The position of assistant minister of the interior and chief of the security sector is a public function. Through the media in the 1990s I frequently heard of General Djordjevic's activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you have told us that in 1998 and 1999 you were the chief of the security department in the Pristina Corps command. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not of the security department, but the security section of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: The security section. All right. And I believe you've said that before that beginning in 1993 you were the deputy chief of the security section in the Pristina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Between 1993 and 1996 I was deputy chief of the security section in the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: At what point in 1998 did you become chief?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't become chief in 1998. It was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. So in the testimony when you've been asked whether you were chief in 1998 and 1999, that was the position you held but you had assumed it even earlier; is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. When in 1996 did you become chief?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of April, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. And you said that one of the tasks of the security section was providing security for the corps commanders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the tasks of the security section of the Pristina Corps is providing security detail for senior officials and officers, including the corps commander when stationary and in movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So who else did the security sector provide security for? And we can talk specifically about 1999. So there was General Lazarevic, the Pristina Corps commander. Who else?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security section was tasked with providing security to the corps commander as well as the Chief of Staff of the corps. There is a list of persons who are -- provided security when stationary and in movement, and these two people are on the top of the list. However, this is done through military police units that I was in charge of professionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. And that leads to my next question: What was your role in terms of providing security for these people, you specifically?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the security section of the command of the Pristina Corps there are two assistant chiefs, that is to say my assistants. One assistant is in charge of counter-intelligence. He is there to put in measures aimed at preventing agents from functioning. The other assistant is for security and staff affairs who, professionally speaking, is in charge of military police units. That assistant uses military police units in order to provide security to the persons enjoying protection; in this case, the corps commander and the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So the security detail itself came from the military police unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, were you responsible for assigning that security detail on a day-to-day basis based on where General Lazarevic was?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not one of my duties. It was a duty of my assistant for staff and security affairs. With appropriate checks, the most reliable personnel was chosen with the assistance of the person in charge of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. So I believe you testified in Milutinovic - correct me if I'm wrong - but it wasn't necessary for you to know where General Lazarevic was every day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I still claim that. It is not an obligation of a superior to report to his subordinate; it is the other way around. When General Lazarevic let me know of his whereabouts, then, of course, I was aware of it, but in certain situations as my superior he was under no obligation to inform me of his activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, during the period of the NATO bombing, did the security sector under your guidance provide security for the 3rd Army commander, General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. General Pavkovic, commander of the 3rd Army, during the NATO bombing when he was within the area of responsibility of the Pristina Corps was always escorted by his security detail from the 3rd Military Police Battalion, which is under the command of the 3rd Army and stationed in Nis. I had certain obligations to fulfill only if there were requests put in to expand his security detail. We would provide assistance to the security detail of General Pavkovic, and we would select people from the Pristina Corps and its MP battalion. However, such requests came in seldom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: What would cause something like that to take place, you being requested to expand the security detail of General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A cause could be that there was a threat to General Pavkovic's safety and security. This could have come about if he were travelling to Kosovo, touring certain units which were close to combat areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So you said this happened seldom. About how many times did this happen?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly. Say whenever General Pavkovic was in the border belt or when he had to go from Kosovo to the area of Metohija, since all roads were exposed to Albanian terrorist attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So are we talking about something closer to one or two times that his security needed to be expanded, or was it something more like 10, 15 times?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the NATO aggression, General Pavkovic quite rarely visited front-line units in Metohija. I believe that was quite seldom. If you're expecting me to tell you how many times exactly, that's really something I can't recall now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And I assume if you did not need to know General Lazarevic's schedule every day, you probably didn't need to know it for General Pavkovic either; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't need to be familiar with the schedule of General Pavkovic and his activities, since he was commander of the 3rd Army. He was not under the competence of my security service. According to the regulation, I should have been familiar with the activities of General Lazarevic, but it was his discretionary right to decide whether he would ask of me as his security chief to provide a military policeman for his escort or not. It was up to him whether he would inform me of his whereabouts at any point in time. That was his right as commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, aside from regulations, what we're interested in here in this courtroom is what, in fact, took place. Did you, in fact, know where General Lazarevic was on most days? Did he inform you of that or did you, in fact, not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Lazarevic throughout the NATO aggression had a squad of military policemen which did not change. They were always escorting him. If there was greater risk in his movement calling for additional people, he would turn to me asking for that. So it was the same unit, the same people who constantly escorted and provided security to General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So just to be clear, other than those occasions when he requested special security from you, you didn't need to be tracking his whereabouts; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. During your time in Kosovo, did you work closely with General Pavkovic? And I'm speaking about your whole time in Kosovo, from 1993 until 1999.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked with General Pavkovic beginning with 1996 because he came to Kosovo and Metohija in 1996 to assume the position of the chief of operations organ in the command of the Pristina Corps. For a while General Pavkovic as the corps commander was my direct superior following that period. As with all other of his assistants, I also co-operated with General Pavkovic professionally. In January 1999, when he was appointed commander of the 3rd Army, my contacts with General Pavkovic ceased.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: They ceased entirely?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not entirely. Not until -- well, occasionally we met by chance or if he visited a certain unit while I was there we had regular contact. But all contact with General Pavkovic did cease in 2000 when I completed the national defence school, when I was assigned to another duty not within the security service, although up to that time my entire career was in that service.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Would you say based on your working relationship with General Pavkovic which started in 1996, did he respect you as far as you know.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Pavkovic respected my professional attitude.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Did he listen to what you had to say?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part he accepted our proposals, but it was his right - as any commander's - not to have to accept them. He had to listen and acknowledge our proposal, but he didn't necessarily have to adopt them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Was it your perception that he generally took you seriously?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: What kind of a leader was General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Pavkovic, whom I've met in 1996 as I've already said, is one of the best staff officers of the army of the FRY. I can freely state that, given the fact that I was stationed in ten garrisons throughout my career; therefore, I had numerous superiors. He was quite courageous, given the fact that during the time when he was the corps commander he frequently went to the front lines where there was combat. But as any other person, he had flaws as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Would you say that you were close to him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, General Pavkovic was never that close to the security service. I think the roots of this situation reach back into a period that preceded his arrival in Kosovo and Metohija, at least that's what I was told. He had some trouble with the security service during his time in the Belgrade garrison, as far back as that. Therefore, he did not have any strong positive feelings about the security service generally speaking or indeed about me because I was part of that service. There is a widespread opinion in the VJ that given the nature of the job done by the security service it might end up harming some people were they to make a misstep. This was the feeling that prevailed among a certain group of officers, and General Pavkovic belonged to that group.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And that's because you're supposed to report on them if they do anything wrong, is that correct, or commit a crime? Let's be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Each of our members, regardless of the rank or level, were under an obligation as soon as they realised that a crime had been committed to immediately report this, and this obviously pertained to any command level at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: During your time in Kosovo, did you work closely with General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was close with General Lazarevic. Every time you perform some tasks, for example, in an army setting, in a military setting, you're likely to work better with some people and not so well with others. You could say that I worked well with General Lazarevic, and I would call him a top-notch professional.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And were the two of you close?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I always did my best to keep my relationships with my superiors perfectly in compliance with the regulations and professional standards. I tried not to take things to a private level. I was subordinated to both General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic. I had respect for them as my superiors, and I would regularly keep them informed on anything that was going on in my own domain.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I think we need to clarify something here. On the previous page, page 11, line 22, I believe your answer -- when I asked whether you worked closely with General Lazarevic your answer was: "Yes, I was close with General Lazarevic." And I believe you just told us you were not close with General Lazarevic. I think we should clarify. Are you saying that you were close with him in terms of a working relationship but not personally close outside of work? Or can you just clarify in your own words?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm in a position to fully confirm what you have just suggested. I was close with him in terms of our professional lives. Nevertheless, I did not privately socialise with him outside work.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Would you in your perception say that General Lazarevic respected you professionally?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And he would listen to what you had to say?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. As chief of the Pristina Corps security section, who specifically would you receive reports from?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As chief of the security section of the Pristina Corps, I would receive reports from my direct subordinates from the security organ in a purely technical sense. The security organs of subordinate brigades in this specific case, those from subordinated battalions. After July 1998 a forward command post was set up in the Djakovica garrison. There was always an experienced operative working there who would regularly submit reports from this forward command post. As for the Pristina Corps brigades, there was several combat groups that were set up. In each of these combat groups there were security organs, and it was their duty to report back to the brigade security officer. And then the brigade security chief would come back to me with all this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So each brigade stationed around Kosovo had officers within it who were part of the security organ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each brigade from the Pristina Corps stationed in Kosovo and Metohija had an officer who was the chief of the security organ, then there would be an administrator, another officer or normally an NCO. And whenever combat groups were set up, they would have an officer or an NCO within them who worked there as a security officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So the combat security -- the security officers in the combat unit would report up to the brigade level, and then all of those security officers in the various brigades would report up to you; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And how often would this reporting occur?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have pointed out several times while giving evidence now and earlier, there was an obligation for security chiefs in the brigades every morning and every evening to use their communications equipment and submit their reports to me. Every time an anti-terrorist operation was completed, they had to submit a written report on the progress of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I just want to make sure I'm understanding this. Outside of when there was a terrorist operation, were they still reporting to you every day and night, or was that only when there was a terrorist operation, an anti-terrorist operation, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each and every day throughout 1998 and 1999, both mornings and evenings, they were submitting to me oral reports, telegrams, and such documents as envisaged by the Rules of Service. These regulated reports, if you like, would normally follow their oral reports. Then they would put together a telegram and this would be followed by a batch of original documents, normally much more extensive. The methodology of our work sets out exactly how they arrived at this information, what sort of information they had, what methods they used while obtaining this information, what was the reliability of the information, how they processed the information or what they did with it, what was their assessment, what was their analysis, what measures were they proposing, and what requests were they making vis-à-vis the security section of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So is it accurate to say that you would get a phone all every morning and every evening followed by these other things that you've just spoken of?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were oral reports, and as I said these were followed by written reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And what type of information were these officers in the security organs supposed to report to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their duty was to inform me about any security-related intelligence in a unit or in a zone of responsibility. Each brigade-level unit in Kosovo and Metohija had its own zone of responsibility. Those security organs that covered the border belt, or rather, the Albanian border had the duty to report on the situation along the borderline as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: When you say "security-related intelligence," what does that include?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to explain. Let us take the example of an anti-terrorist operation. The security officer would be under an obligation to talk to me in the morning, to tell me that on such and such a day such and such an operation was planned involving such and such forces, the objective being this or being that. And then that same evening the operation would normally be completed. The brigade chief would talk to me to tell me about the progress of the operation, were any of our soldiers killed, what were the steps taken by the Siptar terrorists, were any of them taken, were there any unlawful actions committed by the army during the operation, were there any instances of poor command. Their duty was to do this by mail as soon as possible. They were to submit a detailed written report on any operation at all that was launched and completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So one of their responsibilities is to report to you whether there was any criminal conduct or misbehaviour on the part of the VJ soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Any issues at all that had to do with the work of the military security service.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, during times when there was not an operation going on, what kind of information would you get in these morning and evening reports? Would you get intelligence information about the KLA from these people?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This wasn't really intelligence information. The military intelligence service was in charge of that. I was in the counter-intelligence section, the security section, which is different. In such situations my subordinate security organs would be under an obligation to submit oral and written reports to me, much the same as before. But now these reports for the most part concerned the situation across the units because some soldiers would be wounded, there were disciplinary infractions, sometimes criminal offences. Nevertheless, when there was no operation that was underway these reports would normally relate to such intelligence as was gathered concerning certain locations, concerning manpower, concerning the composition of the Albanian terrorists or indeed their intentions and objectives.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you about the relationship between the security section and the military police battalions for a bit. Now, yesterday you said that primarily in the Pristina Corps when we speak about the military police we are speaking about the 52nd Military Police Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. In addition to the 52nd Military Police Battalion, and I'm talking about 1998, please, bear that in mind, in the Pristina Corps there were another two military police companies, A-class military police companies, one of them with the 549th Motorised Brigade in the Prizren garrison, and that was its name, the 549th Military Police Company. The other A-class unit was with the 125th Motorised Brigade and it was called the 125th Military Police Company. On the eve of the NATO aggression, in addition to these two brigades that within their establishment had military police companies, all the other brigades to immobilise their own military police companies, meaning each brigade had a military police company in it and these were subordinated to their respective brigade commanders. The 52nd Military Police Battalion was a unit attached to the corps, but it was independent. It was a corps unit that was independent and directly subordinated to the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Directly subordinated to the Pristina Corps commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday -- actually, I believe this was two days ago now, that the military security service is technically in charge of the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The military security service is in charge of counter-intelligence work and staff security work in any unit including the 52nd Battalion of the military police. In an operative sense, if that's what you're asking and I'll try to simplify, who exactly did security work in the 52nd Military Police Battalion --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that was my --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Let me just clarify, sir, on the 22nd of February on page 7 of the transcript, I realise these now have page numbers, but it's page 7 of that day, at line 14 you were asked: "What are the competences of powers of the military security services vis-à-vis the police?" And you answered: "The military security service is technically in charge of the military police and its work, the technical aspects of the work of the military police." And I'm just asking you to confirm: Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll clarify. Right now your question was: What about in an operative sense? Who did security work in the 52nd Battalion? And that's what I was trying to explain. It was my assistant for staff security, who even in a technical sense would have been in charge of supplying the appropriate equipment and training military police units, generally speaking, as well as any personnel-related matters. In a technical sense, yes, it was in charge of military police units, not just the 52nd Battalion but also all the other companies across the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, I believe two days ago you told us that security officers including you can't order a single unit, even a military police unit; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely fair, yes. This is about deciding on the unit's involvement, on its use. Military security officers had no power or authority over any units, including any military police unit. Only the brigade commander could have issued any orders. As for the 52nd Battalion, only the commander of the Pristina Corps had the power to issue any orders to it because the unit was directly subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, in Milutinovic you explained - and this is at page 162 of that exhibit, your Milutinovic testimony - that the security service proposed the use of units of the military police; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And I'll read a little more here. In your Milutinovic transcript at page 5, line 15, you stated: "The organs of the military security service in technical and professional terms are in charge of the military police organs." Then you were asked: "Do the military security service organs have the right to issue orders to the military police?" You answered: "No, only the commander of the unit that has military police units within its formation has the right to do so. The military security service organs proposed to the commander of such a unit how the military police units are to be -- should be used." Is that your statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at Prosecution Exhibit 1341. Now, sir, these are minutes of the collegium of the VJ General Staff for 25 February 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And if we could just go to page 15 in English and I believe page 15 in the B/C/S, although I had a difficult time matching this up. But I believe it's page 15 and if it's not I'm sure my learned friend will let me know if he's not seeing the same thing. If we could go to the bottom of the page on page 15 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: We see that General Dimitrijevic is about to speak. Now, at this time what was the position of General Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel-General Aleksandar Dimitrijevic at the time was the chief of the security administration of the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So he was your superior's superior; is that fair to say, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me just check with Mr. Djurdjic, are you seeing where General Dimitrijevic is about to speak? We have the right page? All right, thank you. If we could go in the English to the next page where we actually see what he says. He says: "With respect to the departure of an anti-terrorist battalion from the 72nd Special Brigade for KiM, I found it inappropriate that nobody had every consulted me about it. I had been informed about a written order and the dispatch of the best anti-terrorist unit only after it had arrived down there. These initial moves demonstrate that this unit will not be used properly. Part of the unit has been resubordinated to the 52nd" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: "... has been resubordinated ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing. Page 14 in the Serbian, that is what my learned friend is reading from, because it goes on at page 15. Dimitrijevic appears on page 14 of the Serbian, which is what my learned friend is currently reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you for the record, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And just not to read too much of this, going down General Curcin speaks and then we hear briefly from General Ojdanic, and then Dimitrijevic says again: "At any rate, it is clearly stipulated that police units are to be used at our proposal, and we presumably know better than anyone else to what use these units can be put. My only objection was that we should be consulted." Now, in looking at this, sir, would you agree with me that the security sector took seriously their ability to propose the use of these military police units?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may explain the essence of what General Dimitrijevic said here. You see, while giving evidence yesterday I said that the anti-terrorist battalion, being one of the battalions belonging to the 72nd Special Brigade during the NATO aggression, was resubordinated to the 3rd Army and then to the Pristina Corps. Given the fact that the military security service essentially under the regulations has three channels or lines of work, as it were, one of them being counter-intelligence, the other being terrorism, and the third line of work being organised crime, if you look at number 2, terrorism, the security service would make proposals to the appropriate commands concerning the use of anti-terrorist units. In the case at hand, General Dimitrijevic's observation here boils down to what follows. Why was the unit detached from the 72nd Brigade and attached or seconded to the Pristina Corps, resubordinated to it, without him being consulted? Let me remind you of this, nevertheless, the Guards Brigade, the 72nd Special Brigade and the Parachuters Brigade were part of another corps which was called the Special Forces Corps. This Special Forces Corps was stationed in Belgrade. What he's saying here is observing to General Ojdanic or complaining to General Ojdanic, who was Chief of the General Staff at the time, which boils down to the following: Why was the anti-terrorist battalion resubordinated and sent away without his prior consent? And then if you go to the last line he openly complains about the following. He says: I think the expert, the Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army probably made that proposal and who does he have in mind there? He means Colonel-General Ljubisa Stojmirovic, who before he took up his post as Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army was commander of the Special Forces Corps. So what is Dimitrijevic saying here? That General Stojmirovic got the Chief of the General Staff to have that battalion sent or resubordinated to the Pristina Corps, making General Dimitrijevic himself quite unimportant in the process.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And it appears that he is re-asserting the right of the security sector to propose how those military police units are used, correct? He's making clear that he should have been consulted about this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here is what he's saying: He should have been consulted, but not necessarily asked. It is an inviable right for any commander to take a decision because General Dimitrijevic was actually General Ojdanic's subordinate, and the battalion could not be sent away without a decision from the Chief of the General Staff. Therefore, General Ojdanic need not necessarily have asked him. If we talk about military rules or behaviour, if we talk about good business practice and communication, he could have opted to ask him to consult with him, but he was certainly under no obligation to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you were shown a number of telegrams --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'm finished with this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: You were shown a number of telegrams from the Pristina Corps security section, which I believe is you, and the 3rd Army security section. A lot of these were in the form of telegrams; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could look at D749, please, the first page -- first we'll look at the first page in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were shown this two days ago, and it appears that this is a Pristina Corps command security department telegram from 19th of December, 1999 [sic]; am I accurate on that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And if we could look at the last page in B/C/S, e-court page number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I note that there's no signature on this page; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. If you want me, I'll explain. Most telegrams do not have a signature. That is why originals are kept in the archives. When I draft this telegram late in the evening and summarise a report for the command for that day, I then give the text to those in the code department responsible for encoding it and sending it on to this superior command. They receive my telegram in this version, but I guarantee that all this information is original and true. You can see my initials there, meaning that I drafted the telegram, as I did most of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So you would say that this copy of the telegram is an authentic copy of your telegram, even though it has no signature?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is completely authentic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yesterday -- or actually, I'm -- you've got two days of testimony, so sometimes I'm not sure if it was yesterday or the day before, but at some point in your testimony the last two days when we were looking at these Pristina Corps security department telegrams, it appeared that a number of these telegrams contained information from the state security department or section; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We exchanged information regularly. Some information came from the State Security Service, some information was our own, some came from the 14th counter-intelligence group. I would put that all together in a single telegram.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could look at Prosecution 65 ter 02945.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that is happening, page 23, line 21, you gave the date of the last exhibit as 19th of December, 1999. I think it should be 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: You're very correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, is that a picture of you in this article?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And is this an interview you gave to the Nedeljni Telegraf on, I believe it is the 22nd of November, 2000?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. If we could look at page 5 in the English and in B/C/S on page 4, the first full paragraph in the first column. And the type is very small in the B/C/S so I will read this out because I'm not sure if you'll be able to make it out. Now, this article you're criticising the MUP and some others for failing to adequately address terrorism in Kosovo as it built up in the 1990s. And on page 5, midway through the second paragraph in the English it says: "That which is true is that the state security delivered some information to the army about the directions of the entry of terrorists and weapons from Albania to Kosovo across the border. However, I responsibly claim that the majority of the information was not true. Acting on that information in a certain number of cases, we engaged significant forces, but it almost always turned out that that was not necessary, by which we were exhausting the people and maybe leaving some other directions of entry open. Not once the question was asked to which degree was reliable and verified the information that they would provide us with sometimes." Is that your statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my statement. Perhaps I should clarify something. There were frequent situations in which representatives of the State Security Service forwarded information, stating that along a certain route towards Albania there was supposed to be a convoy of beasts of burden of sorts carrying weapons, and then we had to allocate certain units from our combat disposition to set up ambushes and spend all night there. On several occasions such information proved incorrect because there were simply no terrorists passing there. This further exhausted our forces, and this is what I was referring to in the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like to ask you a little bit about your role in the Pristina Corps command. You were part of the Pristina Corps command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. And what meetings did you attend related to that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have in mind the question in the interview or the meetings of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm not asking you about the exhibit at this point. Just -- I'm asking you about a new topic now. And I should be a little more precise. I mean regular meetings. I'm sure you had various meetings here and there, but what regular meetings were you part of as part of the Pristina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By function I was a member of the Pristina Corps commanders' collegium comprising the Chief of Staff of the corps, the chief of the operations department, assistant commander for logistics, assistant commander for morale, chief of the security section, as well as assistant commander for garrison affairs. As for the meetings of the collegium of the corps commander, these were held during 1998 regularly. And after the NATO aggression, there were never such comprehensive meetings with all of those people in attendance. During 1998 I briefed on all security aspects in the units and information I gathered in the field. I also carried out analyses and proposed measures to the corps commander. In 1999 the Pristina Corps command was never in a single location. It was dispersed per or by command organs. For example, the logistics organ was in one location, the morale organ and second operations organ on a third location. They were all in the general area of Pristina. Therefore, due to the air-strikes and constantly changing situation in units, movements, as well as numerous problems of the corps, it was impossible to have full collegium meetings. During 1999 there were meetings, though, of the corps of the collegium. For example, when decisions needed to be made, the Chief of Staff and the commander would meet and they would call us individually if they needed any of us to join them. Also, on -- of my own initiative when I had information that were of significant security interest, I was under an obligation to locate the commander and convey it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Did you know about actions that the Pristina Corps had planned for its units in your role?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. I received certain information from the operations organ who was supposed to plan such actions and draw maps, but if I didn't know when such actions were planned at least I was always informed of such actions after their taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Did you take part in any capacity in planning the actions of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the staff part when a plan is drawn up is something I never participated in, but I did participate in activities before any decisions are made. Whenever asked, I was supposed to provide a security assessment in certain locations where the action was supposed to take place. I was supposed to provide information on the presence of terrorists, their personnel numbers, weapons, plans, deployment, as well as information on any fortifications. I forwarded such information to the operational affairs organ, who kept that in mind when planning the operation. He needed to decide which forces we needed and in which manner such an action would be executed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: This seems like pretty important information to have before an anti-terrorist action, do you agree, know what you're going up against?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anti-terrorist actions were not planned solely based on my information. There was also information coming from the staff in Kosovo and Metohija as well as information from the state and public security sector and the 14th counter-intelligence group, which was under -- which was not under my command. Some information also came from the security organs of the military district which was under the command of the 3rd Army. Some information also came from field commanders who encountered terrorists all the time. In addition to the counter-intelligence service there was also an intelligence service in the Pristina Corps command. When all that information found its way to the operations organ, it was only then that they would start drawing up plans for a specific anti-terrorist action.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, these other sources of information, were some of these channelled through you? All of these individual people weren't coming to meet with the Pristina Corps command, were they? Was it channelled through you to pass on that information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I apologise. It seems that this microphone is off. My answer is no. Information coming from the 14th counter-intelligence group and intelligence organs as well as security organs of the military district, including information from the state and public security sector did not need necessarily go through my hands for me to forward them to the organs of the Pristina Corps. It is true that I exchanged information with them, but it was possible for the Pristina Corps command to call the chief of the state security sector and ask him for an assessment. He could also call the commander of the 14th counter-intelligence group to receive information. We did exchange information, but it wasn't necessary to have all of them, in particular the intelligence organs because they were separate and they followed a different method since the assistant commander for intelligence affair was also subordinated to the commander of the Pristina Corps. He informed him of the situation in Albania, about the border belt, as well as all the other issues that fall within their remit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm speaking specifically about the planning of an operation and your role in assisting that. Are you telling us that before an operation, instead of just getting information from you about the security situation that they would hear from all these various groups about all their information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For the most part they received information from the security section of the Pristina Corps, and they relied heavily on that information because that information was most of the time correct. But the commander had the right to seek opinion from the field commanders as well as other organs. However, the biggest part of information came from the security section of the Pristina Corps in terms of possible planning of any anti-terrorist action.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And just to help clarify this, I think your testimony, sir, in the Milutinovic case at page 143, you were asked: "Did you participate in the preparation or plans for combat actions or manoeuvres of the various units of the Pristina Corps?" And you said: "I participated in the part which related to giving over information and providing knowledge about the locations, plans, intentions, strength of the Albanian terrorists, and that information I sent to the chief of the department for operations of the corps command." Is that a fair statement of your role and planning in assisting in the plans for operations?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see nothing in dispute. There is no difference between what I said then and now. The operations department and its chief serve as the brain when it comes to any planning of operations by the Pristina Corps. As I said then I say now, that I forwarded information to the chief of operations who would then follow it up with the core of the command and the corps commander because not the entire command participated, only those officers for whom the corps commander believed he needed for a specific operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And it seems that it would be important for this information to be as up-to-date as possible; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information was always up-to-date. In my view, we had very able personnel. I believe our information was very reliable throughout 1998 and 1999. Of course it's a different matter as to what use that information was put. After the war certain terrorist leaders published a number of books, such as the book of Ramush Haradinaj, and by having read that I was able to conclude that at the time we had very good information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And I'm asking you something slightly different. I don't doubt that your information was very up-to-date. I'm asking you -- it was important for the commanders and the command of the Pristina Corps to get that most up-to-date information for that anti-terrorist action, is that fair to say, for them to know this information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in full. They always wanted information, and we were always in the field, so the pace of work was very fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So before an anti-terrorist operation they would probably need to know things like: Have the terrorists shifted positions? Have they gained reinforcement? Have they gotten better weapons? Things like that, that would be important to pass on?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is partially true. It is true that they needed to have the type of information you specified; however, primarily they had to know the locations, which settlements, which geographical and topographic features are held by the terrorists and by what means and forces. They needed to know about their system of defence in terms of engineering and mining. They needed to know who is in command, the manning levels, and the type of weapons. They needed to know what the force morale was and what those forces planned to do in the ensuing period. They also needed to know whether there were experts, so to say, foreign mercenaries or instructors from other countries such as was the case. We also needed to know what were their pull-out routes and links to other terrorist staffs. This was a host of problems and issues that was always kept up-to-date, and it was constantly assessed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And the command would need to know that information as of right then, not two weeks ago or even a week ago; they would need to know what is the situation with regard to those things right now. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, daily and in real time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I see we have reached the time for the break. Before we do, I would seek to tender Prosecution 65 ter 02945.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01543.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first break now resuming at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my inadequate explanation concerning an administrative question was apparently not sufficiently clear. I believe I should leave it to Ms. O'Leary to explain what this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Things are best left in the hands of experts, Mr. Djurdjic. I'm learning that every day. Ms. O'Leary.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. While I don't claim to be an expert, I will say that what we were seeking was leave of the Trial Chamber to replace D723, which is under seal, and D724, which are the trial transcripts from Milutinovic et al. of this witness, Mr. Stojanovic. The ones that were entered into evidence on Monday actually were missing the 11 December 2007 transcript in its entirety. So we've reloaded them at the numbers given by Mr. Djurdjic this morning. So we're just seeking a ruling from the Trial Chamber to replace those in evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, that is granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, in your Milutinovic transcript you said at page 5, line 5: "The organs of the military security service participate in the actions that precede the institution of criminal proceedings." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That was my fault.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: In layman terms, sir, does that mean you would -- you in your section would investigate crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that I and my department or the members of my department, as soon as we found out about a crime that occurred, would first inform our superiors, after which we would take such steps and measures as were required to initiate criminal proceedings, the objective being to arrest the perpetrator or at least keep the perpetrator from escaping. It means securing the crime scene, it means gathering any information that might prove helpful in shedding light on the commission of the crime. And if the perpetrator was arrested and handed over to the appropriate judicial authorities, we would then follow any further orders and requests by the investigating magistrate.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So you would secure the crime scene; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And when you say it means gathering any information that might be helpful, does that include both interviewing potential witnesses and gathering physical evidence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And what was your responsibility with regard to that evidence? Would you keep the evidence secure?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would normally familiarise the relevant judicial authority or prosecutor with the evidence, and the evidence would then be duly handed over to the appropriate judicial authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, how was an investigation - and I'm using the term "investigation" to basically describe what you just spoke of, is that a fair word, "investigation," to describe what your unit was doing during this period?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that term is not entirely appropriate, but gathering appropriate information and gathering evidence that might help shed light on a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So, sir, we don't have to repeat all that, would you agree with me that we can use the word "investigation," and it will mean what you just said? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. How was an investigation triggered?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An investigation would normally be preceded by gathering information to the effect that a specific crime was committed. After that a team would go to inspect the scene, secure the scene, and carry out investigative steps. And then the forensic team would draw up a criminal report. Any persons potentially having knowledge of the crime would be interviewed. Statements would be taken and recorded. Any other items or objects might be gathered that could help with the investigation of the crime in question. There was a whole set of steps and rules to be followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: In the very first instance, how did you learn of a potential crime that needed to be investigated?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two ways -- or rather, there were many ways. Sometimes a commander in a unit would report a crime or else any member of a certain unit would report a crime or else we would use our operatives to receive -- in the units to receive intelligence indicating that a crime was committed without the relevant superior officer in that unit necessarily being aware of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Just so I am sure I understand, when you talk about your operatives in the unit, are those the people who are within the security organ, or are you talking about people who were acting as operatives unbeknownst to the unit?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organs of any unit - and this applies to any service or indeed any army in the world - work more or less in keeping with the same methods. There is a methodology that is prescribed in terms of gathering information and intelligence. One of the ways to go about this is through agents or associates. That's what we called them. These positions, so to speak, existed in all units. Wherever there was something going on and wherever there could be expected some enemy activity, within the army or against the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So these associates within the units would tell you if some of the troops, for example, were actually meeting with the KLA and were possibly going to desert; would that be an example?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They would tell us that whenever they had information like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, you said that the security organs in the brigades would report up to you every day and night. Was that a source of learning about any crimes that were committed by VJ units?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That worked through my subordinates, the security organs in the brigades, and that was my basis for establishing whether a crime was committed or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So you've listed, just to make sure I have this all, getting information from your subordinates in the security organs within those units; possibly a commander would tell you that one of his troops had committed a crime; or an officer may come forward and say that a crime was committed; or your associates may say something is going on in the unit. Were those your basic sources of information that would then lead to an investigation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, or else we could use the chain of command. As you suggested, one of the commanders comes forward and reports this to his own security chief. To me, for example, or his own brigade security chief. Or the security officers would do their work in the unit, they would receive information like that, and they would go up the chain and report it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: What types of crime were within your sector's authority and competence to investigate?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any type of crime committed in the line of duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So primarily you were looking -- or maybe exclusively, correct me so that I'm accurate. You were looking at crimes committed by the VJ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially true, yes. Any crimes committed by the VJ, committed by any member of the VJ, but also including those crimes committed against the unit commands, institutions, or members of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And so in those instances primarily you would be talking about terrorists or others who tried to subvert the VJ; is that an accurate description?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Enemy activity and illegal activity against the army was not a thing that pertained to terrorists alone. There was a broad spectrum. You had illegal intelligence activity, terrorist activity, links between organised crime from that area and some members of the army. There were regulations governing the work of security organs detailing the procedures. It wasn't just about any crimes committed by the terrorists targeting army units or army commands. This covered all of the other crimes committed within the army or indeed against the army, thus a broad spectrum.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I have sort of a general question that I just want to make sure I understand. It seems in your description of your job you have two important functions. One of them is intelligence or possibly counter-intelligence, I'm not sure how you would describe it, intelligence of information that may be harmful to the VJ such as KLA activity or whether other people are meeting with the KLA or whether troops within the VJ are doing something disloyal. So you have that one the one hand. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The work of the security service breaks down in the roughest of terms into two sections. One is counter-intelligence. I spoke about that a while ago. This is key. Nearly 90 per cent of our activity comes down to that. This is, to be perfectly clear, military counter-intelligence. So that's the counter-intelligence component. And then the breakdown within counter-intelligence is as follows: Preventing any agents from taking action against the army, any army facilities or members, or against the country's defence as a whole. The other component is unclosing -- monitoring and intercepting any terrorist activity within the army or indeed against the army. And the third component is uncovering, monitoring, and intercepting any criminal activity within the army or any links between criminal activity within the army and external factors within the territory. The other function that you asked me about today is really about taking pre-emptive measures within unit commands and institutions, normally those of general significance or broader significance. This has to do with safety and security. For example, running military police units, for example, securing military facilities or high-ranking military persons or preventing the theft of weapons, pre-empting acts of sabotage, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So counter-intelligence includes, for example, your information about the KLA, that would be classic counter-intelligence information; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Are you also including in counter-intelligence gathering information about whether VJ units or troops are engaging in crimes? And when I mean crimes here, I'm not talking about crimes against the army like, you know, treason or desertion. I'm talking about crimes against others, crimes against the population. Do you include that in counter-intelligence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. Now, when we're talking about crimes by the VJ, are you -- is part of your responsibility to investigate any kind of crime committed by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my duty and legal obligation to investigate any illegal activity committed by any member of the army. In a technical sense, yes, it would be something for the military security service.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So that would include crimes against civilians, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: That would include any instance where members of the military murdered a civilian? Would it include that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Rape?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Looting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: How about expelling civilians from their homes, would that be a type of crime committed by a VJ member that you would be responsible for investigating?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, during the period of the NATO bombing and before that in the summer of 1998, the MUP and [Realtime transcript read in error "the movement of] the VJ worked closely together, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And just to correct the transcript, page 41, line 2, it's the MUP, M-U-P, and the VJ worked closely together. Now, during a co-ordinated action between the MUP and the VJ, were security organs in those units supposed to report up to you about any crimes that the MUP might have committed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Again I'll have to take you back to the laws and regulations governing the work of military security organs. The only thing they're in charge is their own members and their own ranks; nevertheless, any person would have been under an obligation including military security officers. As soon as they came across information that there was a crime that someone else committed, to report this to their own superior commander or their own superior officer down the more technical chain. In this case that would have been me. That is, if they ever came across information like that. But it wasn't in their job description to follow that sort of thing. It would have been illegal for them to monitor or follow closely what the MUP people were doing. This was something that was down to the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, we've heard from a Defence witness, Mr. Gojovic, and I believe he spoke about a duty of all officers, all military officers, that if they were aware of a crime they were to report on it. Are you aware of that, or could you assist us with that rule?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to explain. For example, there was a joint action being performed by the MUP and the army. Very often they don't operate along the same axes or indeed in the same areas, rather, they simply co-ordinate. If you have an action like that being performed and now one of the military security men comes across information suggesting that a member of the MUP committed a crime or indeed violated the provisions of international law of war, this person would have been under an obligation to immediately report this to the appropriate army unit commander, the commander of the unit that was involved in the action, and also to report this to the superior security officer, that is, me. And I would be forwarding this information to the appropriate MUP authorities and to the appropriate state security authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. So if a security officer became aware of a MUP crime, they should report that information to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But he has no authority to launch an investigation or indeed take any other steps. This would have been illegal. This would have clashed with the regulations because there were other bodies that were in charge of that, the state security bodies and Ministry of the Interior, of which the State Security Service was a component.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You would agree if in co-ordinated actions where the VJ is supporting the MUP, if in those actions the MUP is repeatedly committing crimes that would be something that's important for you to know, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about this formulation of yours whereby you said the MUP is repeatedly committing crimes. In any case, as I've told you, concerning information on any illegal acts that we received, we were duty-bound to report on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And when this information involved someone from the MUP, once you reported on it do you know what would happen at that point, who would take over?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we received some information of a member of the army committing something like that, then those responsible to undertake measures would be the superior commanders or in this case those competent were organs of the Ministry of the Interior as well as security organs, state security organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And at that point, and I'm speaking specifically about information about the MUP committing crimes, you would not follow it after that point?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were under no legal obligation to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Let's speak for a minute about when you learn of information that a member of the VJ has committed a crime. Can you just tell us specifically once you learned about that and you begin the investigation, how do you -- what's the next step? What then happens with that case?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we learned of an army member having committed a specific crime, we would first inform the competent commander. Second, we would undertake a number of measures to have that perpetrator arrested as quickly as possible so as to prevent him from fleeing. We would also secure the crime scene with the help of military policemen and undertake measures there. If the perpetrator is arrested together with all material evidence and conclusions of an on-site investigation, he is handed over to an investigating judge. If a perpetrator is unidentified or fleeing, we also undertake all measures in terms of collecting evidence and an on-site investigation, and we submit a criminal report against an unidentified perpetrator. Following that, we resume taking measures in order to establish who the perpetrator is and any other follow-up activities which may have to do with the specific crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: When does your role end in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My role in the investigation does not end with the submission of a criminal report and the case file being handed over to the competent court. We would also have to undertake all other measures requested by the investigating judge if a person needed to be brought in, if witness statements needed to be taken, anything that may lead to an official indictment being issued against the perpetrator of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So your section has a role up until the period of indictment. Do you continue having any role up until a particular individual is convicted or their case terminates?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After an indictment is issued, we can only act following an order of the competent prosecutor, otherwise we wouldn't take any other measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, when we just -- when we spoke a minute ago about the obligation of a security officer to report to you if they learned of the MUP committing a crime, how often did that happen during the period of the NATO bombing that you heard from your security officers that the MUP was committing crimes during operations?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably wanted to ask me how frequently that happened --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, how frequently or how many times, if you can estimate that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite seldom. The zones of combat activities of army units did not correspond to the zones of activity of MUP units. Also axes of engagement and the activities in question did not necessarily correspond. Security organs mainly focused on the activities of the army; however, if we got by information of that nature, of which there were very few such as cases of lack of discipline or certain MUP members being found while looting Albanian property, then we advised their group commander who, in turn, was supposed to inform the competent commander of the MUP unit participating in that action.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
